content: 1. The Cochrane Database Systematic Review (2015) evaluated the quality of evidence regarding antenatal care (ANC) interventions. The pooled effect sizes were primarily derived from studies classified as B or C, with less than 40% contribution from C studies. The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to factors such as asymmetry in the funnel plot and unexplained heterogeneity. 2. A comparison between group ANC and individual ANC showed a low certainty of evidence. A single study conducted in the USA, focusing on the Centering Pregnancy model, raised concerns about generalizability. Wide confidence intervals (CIs) crossing the line of no effect and severe heterogeneity further limited the reliability of findings. 3. Community-based interventions, such as women’s groups, home visits, or intervention packages combining home visits and community mobilization, were compared to control groups. The quality of evidence was moderate, but the estimates were crude due to the reliance on cluster randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The inverse variance method was used for meta-analyses, and the findings were influenced by asymmetry in the funnel plot and unexplained heterogeneity. 4. Focused ANC (FANC), which involves a minimum of four visits, was compared to the standard ANC model requiring at least eight visits. The evidence was rated as moderate quality. The analysis relied on cluster RCTs, and the inverse variance method was used. Wide CIs crossing the line of no effect and unexplained heterogeneity were noted as limitations. 5. The World Health Organization (WHO) conducted a systematic search in December 2013 to identify existing ANC guidelines. Databases such as PubMed, LILACS, and TRIP were searched using broad strategies, including terms like pregnancy, antenatal, care, and guidelines. The search was limited to guidelines published after January 2000. A total of 79 eligible guidelines were identified, with additional references obtained through expert input and reference checking. 6. A qualitative meta-synthesis of women’s views on routine ANC included studies using qualitative designs such as ethnography, phenomenology, and grounded theory. The focus was on women’s experiences, attitudes, and barriers to ANC. Studies published between January 2000 and August 2014 were included, with no language restrictions. Abstracts and full texts were translated when necessary. 7. A separate qualitative meta-synthesis examined healthcare providers’ views on delivering routine ANC. This included staff in primary, secondary, and tertiary care settings who met the WHO definition of skilled birth attendants. Studies published between January 2000 and August 2014 were included, with no language restrictions. The findings highlighted facilitators and barriers to providing quality ANC services. 8. The WHO recommendations on ANC for a positive pregnancy experience were informed by systematic reviews and evidence-based guidelines. The search strategies were adapted to fit the syntax of each database, and inclusion/exclusion criteria were applied consistently. The process involved independent review by two team members, with adjudication by a third member in cases of disagreement. 9. Databases such as African Journals Online (AJOL), AMED, CINAHL, Embase, and PsycINFO were searched for relevant studies. Zetoc alerts were set up for over 50 journals to ensure comprehensive coverage. The search terms included keywords related to participants, areas of interest, and study designs, ensuring a broad and inclusive approach. 10. The 2016 WHO ANC model emphasized large-scale program evaluations. Searches for peer-reviewed literature were conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and Embase. Grey literature was also included to capture all relevant evidence.
